result:
You have never seen your own face.

This sounds like a riddle, but it's simply true. Everything you know about your appearance is secondhand: mirrors (which reverse you), photographs (which flatten and freeze you), the reactions of others (which interpret you). The face — the thing most intimately yours, the thing people recognize across a crowded room — is permanently offscreen from your point of view. You are the only person who will never watch your own smile happen.

There's something almost tender in this arrangement. Your face, it turns out, was never really for you. It's an instrument pointed outward, broadcasting emotion to everyone else while you receive only the internal buzz of feeling. You know your delight from the inside; everyone else knows it from the outside; and the two never meet in a single view.

We adapt strangely. Because mirrors dominate our self-image, the reversed version feels like the "real" one — which is why photographs often look subtly wrong. Even video calls only hand you a delayed, lens-bent copy. The face your friends know is a mild stranger to you.

Philosophers have made much of the gap between how we appear and how we know ourselves. But maybe the simpler lesson is this: some of what we are exists only in other people's eyes. We spend our lives being seen, trusting that the face we can't watch is doing its quiet, expressive work.

When someone says "you look happy today," they're reporting news from a country you can never visit.
